His elder son Mukesh Ambani took the legacy forward and added other businesses including telecom business launched in 2016 called Jio. Today. his son Akash Ambani took it to a newer heights by going for an IPO, which replicated his grandfather, Dhirubhai. 

But its the Reliance Power IPO of Anil Ambani released in 2008, which holds the record of the fastest subscribed IPO

Reliance power ushered in the bear market in India that lasted for 6 years

The cost of Winning ft. INSTAHELP  vs BLINKIT

There is a part of the "winner-take-all" story in quick commerce that I think is worth remembering as we look at Urban Company’s InstaHelp.

Blinkit is often used as proof that quick commerce eventually works. And it does show that a player can go through years of heavy investment and losses and eventually build a profitable business at scale.

But there is another side to that story.

In Q4 FY26, Zepto reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹1,248 Cr and Swiggy Instamart reported a loss of ₹858 Cr, while Blinkit reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹37 Cr.

The point isn't that Zepto or Instamart will fail. It is that a winner-take-most market can require enormous investment from multiple players before the eventual economics become clear.

And this is exactly what makes Urban Company's InstaHelp interesting.

Urban Company has explicitly said that InstaHelp is its most significant long-term investment. In Q4 FY26, it reported a ₹119 Cr adjusted EBITDA loss in the business and said losses would remain elevated as it invested to cement leadership.

By Q1 FY27, the loss had increased to ₹132 Cr, even as orders grew 43% QoQ to 3.82 million and loss per order improved from ₹447 to ₹346.

That is the interesting tension.

If this really is a winner-take-all or winner-take-most market, then being early and building density could matter enormously.

But winning also means being willing to fund the network before the economics fully show up.

Urban Company's bet is essentially that density creates a flywheel: more demand → better partner utilisation → better earnings → better supply retention → faster fulfilment → more demand.

If that flywheel works, today's losses could be investments in future market structure.

If it doesn't, the same losses simply become the cost of competing in an attractive category.

That's why I wouldn't look at InstaHelp's ₹132 Cr quarterly loss in isolation.

I'd watch whether each additional rupee of investment is buying greater density, utilisation and repeat behaviour -and whether those improvements eventually translate into structurally better unit economics OR  eventual market leadership position.

That's the real test of the winner-take-all thesis.
Not whether Urban Company can grow fast. Whether it can turn the cost of winning into an economic moat.

Religion and Science
Religion and Science are diametrically opposed to each other. They are poles apart, and it is nonsense to say that they compliment each other.

1. Religion says that there is a supernatural entity called God, which is immortal, permanent, all powerful, merciful, all good, etc

Science does not believe in supernatural entities. It does not believe anything in the Universe is permanent. Everything is changing and in flux, in accordance with some laws, which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that there are no supernatural entities like God, angels, fairies, demons,witches or soul ( and therefore there is no such thing as transmigration of the soul, or resurrection on Judgment Day ), and that nothing is permanent, everything is changing, and in a state of flux, in accordance with certain laws which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that the only reality is matter, which is in motion according to certain laws.
Some people ask : who created matter ? The answer is : there is no creator of matter. Matter came from matter, though the form keeps changing.

2. With every step science advances, religion recedes. Thus, people at one time thought that small pox is due to the anger of a goddess ( mata ), but now we know it is because of a virus, and can be prevented by innoculation. People at one time thought that rains are caused by a rain god, Indra, and so if there is drought we have to propitiate that god in some way ( many people in India still believe that ). Today we know that rains are caused by the build up of low pressure areas over a heated land. People at one time believed that Adam and Eve were created by God. Later Darwin proved that men evolved from the apes.

3. Religion relies on faith and divine revelation.
Science relies on observation, experiment and reason.

4. Religion claims to say the final word, and cannot be changed. Thus, the Vedas, the Quran, the Bible, etc cannot be changed.
In science there is no final word, and scientific theories can, and have been, regularly tested and changed.

For example, Newton said in 1666 that light travelled as particles ( the corpuscular theory ). But in
1678 the Dutch scientist Huygens' propunded his Fresnel principle that light travelled as waves. Much later Max Planck propounded his Quantum theory which said that light travelled as discrete particles. Still later, Quantum mechanics, as propounded by De Broglie, and as developed by Heisenberg, Schrodinger, etc, said that particles can be conceived of as waves ( and vice versa )

5. Religion says that the Universe was created at a particular time by God, with all living beings. But Darwin proved by his theory of evolution, that creatures have evolved.

6. Religion says that there has to be a Creator of the Universe, which is God.

Science says that there is no such Creator. The only reality in the Universe is matter ( or rather matter-energy, since matter and energy are two forms of the same substance, as Einstein proved ), and matter is in motion, in accordance with certain laws, which can be discovered by scientific research. If it is asked where did matter come from, the answer is matter came from matter.

If it is said that every thing must have a creator, then that creator too must have a creator. i.e. a super creator, and that super creator too must have a creator, i.e. a super super creator, and so on. This is known as the fallacy of the infinite regress.

7. Religion says that God is all powerful, merciful and all good. If that is so, then why do millions of children in the world suffer from hunger, cold, etc ? Why does God, who is said to be merciful, not have mercy on them and give them food, clothes, shelter, etc ?

Why is there so much poverty, unemployment, malnourishment, sickness etc in the world ? If God is
powerful and merciful, why does he not abolish these and give everyone a decent life ?
It is true that some scientists believed in God. But that only proves that scientific and unscientific ideas can co-exist in the same head, and it will take a long time, probably several generations, before unscientific ideas are altogether eliminated

All religions are superstitions and false. The truth lies in science, which is constantly developing.
If India is to progress, we must go over from religion to science

The fog had returned, thicker now, pressing against the railing. Down the path…. the path that, according to Helen, kept shortening, she saw a light. 

Not a lamp. 

A steady, low glow the color of a ship’s lantern seen through rain. It moved slowly, as if someone were walking the waterline, stopping now and then to listen.

Mara stepped off the porch. The boards did not creak. The air smelled of diesel and wet wool. She counted her steps. 

At thirty-one she reached the place where the path should have ended at the rocks. Instead the ground continued, firm under her boots, sloping gently downward. 

The light ahead of her paused. She heard, very clearly, the three strikes of a bell, then two more, closer than any buoy could be.
The light went out.

When she turned, the house was farther away than it should have been. Its windows were dark. The porch lamp she had left burning was gone. In its place, on the top step, sat the brass bell she still held in her hand, or thought she held. Her fingers were empty. 

The bell was on the step, and beside it, written in the thin film of salt the tide had left, were five words in a hand she recognized from the journals…

Do not answer it.

Behind her, out on the water that was no longer water, the bell struck once. Then it waited.
A flashlight beam cut through the fog from the road. “Harbor Police. Don’t move.”

Mara turned. 

A woman in a dark uniform stood at the edge of the yard, badge catching the weak light… Detective Lisa Nazzaro, 381. She kept one hand near her belt and studied the salt-written words, then the bell, then Mara’s empty hands.

“I’m Detective Lisa Nazzaro,” she said. 

Her voice was low, local. “Dispatch got a call about lights on the water and someone walking the point. You the one who inherited Helen’s place?”

Mara nodded. 

The detective’s eyes flicked past her toward the water, where the fog had thickened again. No light showed now.

“Helen called us twice last fall,” Detective Nazzaro said. “Same story. Path shortening. The bell that shouldn’t ring. 

We logged it and told her to stay off the rocks after dark. She stopped calling after that.” The officer stepped closer, boots crunching salt. “You hear it just now?”

“Three, then two,” Mara said. “Then one.”
Detective Nazzaro’s mouth tightened. She reached for her radio, then stopped. The static that came back, was not static. 

Under it, faint and precise, came the same pattern…three strikes, a pause, two more. Closer than the road. Closer than the house.

The detective lowered the radio without answering. She looked at the words in the salt, then at Mara.

“Get inside,” she said. “Lock the door. And whatever you do… please do not answer it.”

From the water the bell struck once more and held the note, waiting.

Mid-Journey——
above a rain-dark street,
the bandoneon breathed into the room.
A floorboard sighed beneath my shoe,
remembering a thousand other dances.

Then your palm settled 
between my shoulder blades——
a pressure scarcely heavier than breath.
I had not decided to move
when my heel began to rise.

Something in your hand had reached
something beneath my skin
before either of us could name it.

We turned. You paused.
In that pause, I felt the next step gathering,
quiet as a tide before it reaches shore.
When I stood still, I sensed your weight shifting;
when you stood still, the unfinished turn
went on turning inside my ribs.

No one had written this music.
A hesitation became a measure,
a breath held open the space between two notes.
We followed a score
our bodies were writing too quickly to read.

Where your hand met my back,
I could no longer tell
which of us had begun to sway.
Yet your hand remained your hand,
and my back, my back——
while the invisible boundary between them
moved with every breath.

Then the bandoneon fell silent.

Footsteps returned across the wooden floor.
But neither of us stepped away.
Beneath the quiet of our skin,
an unfinished measure went on.

And I wondered——
had we been dancing all along,
or was it the distance between us
that had finally learned to dance?

Of all the anachronistic and distorted, straw-man claptrap from @MichealMartinTD. 

How did the drafters of the 1916 proclamation at that time understand the cultural category 'Irish'? As culturally unique—handed down from generations past —and worthy of preservation (essentialism), or as culturally protean?

The opening paragraph of the proclamation strongly suggests cultural  uniqueness:
'In the name of God and of the dead generations from which she receives her old tradition of nationhood, Ireland, through us, summons her children to her flag and strikes for her freedom'.

The second paragraph even more so, as it refers to the undesirable historical impositions by foreign people and governments on Ireland: 
'We declare the right of the people of Ireland to the ownership of Ireland and to the unfettered control of Irish destinies, to be sovereign and indefeasible. The long usurpation of that right by a foreign people and government has not extinguished the right, nor can it ever be extinguished except by the destruction of the Irish people'.

In the decades ensuing the drafting of the proclamation, the drive for de-Anglicisation and re-Gaelicisation of the state—to counter the perceived ill effects of an imposed cultural imperialism—even yet more strongly suggests this pursuit of cultural essentialism or uniqueness by the political and other national establishments. 

It was within this latter cultural context that the drafters naively envisioned a theoretical society where all the nation's citizens would enjoy equality,  oblivious of the constructed differences fostered under historical colonialism and the imposition of an unequal union, then of 115 years standing. 

'The Republic guarantees religious and civil liberty, equal rights and equal opportunities to all its citizens, and declares its resolve to pursue the happiness and prosperity of the whole nation and of all its parts, cherishing all of the children of the nation equally, and oblivious of the differences carefully fostered by an alien Government, which have divided a minority from the majority in the past'.

Did those who drafted the proclamation desire a specifically Irish society and identity, culturally, socially, politically and economically better and more equal than that which preceded it? Certainly.  

Was the utopian dream achieved? No. For one thing a large cohort within the nation had  a different vision for Ireland, and hence partition. And even within the Free State, inequalities and cultural fault lines quickly became apparent. 

The utopian vision of Irishness shifted on the basis of four perceived idyllic purity criteria: Celtic, Irish-speaking, Rural and Catholic. Even sports were contaminated by these cultural constructs. 

Finally, did the proclamation's drafters envision ceding any newly-won sovereignty to foreign powers other than the United Kingdom? Certainly not. 

So the bottom line, @MichealMartinTD, is that you need to own your vision for Ireland and not anachronistically superimpose it on the intents of the proclamation drafters.
